section_summary: This section covers State Department decimal file 894.014 concerning Japanese territorial claims, mandates, boundaries, and cartographic intelligence between January 1940 and December 1944. Major topics include legal status inquiries and strategic planning regarding the Japanese Mandated Islands (Micronesia) and Shinnan Gunto (Spratly Islands), inter-agency coordination with the Joint Chiefs of Staff and military intelligence over Pacific island sovereignty, and administrative territorial adjustments such as the expansion of Kobe. In addition, numerous private citizens and diplomatic posts forwarded seized, tourist, or commercial maps and photographs of Japan and its occupied regions to assist wartime operations.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a telegram concerning Japanese Antarctic claims discussed in the Japanese Diet.
subfiles.from: State Department / Japan
subfiles.summary: A cross-reference sheet referencing Telegram No. 3 from Japan dated January 3, 1940 (filed under 800.014 Antarctic/360). It instructs verifying the reliability of reported discussions in the Japanese Diet concerning Japanese claims in the Antarctic.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Japanese Antarctic Claims

subfiles.about: Inquiry by Professor Roland D. Hussey regarding the sovereignty of Marcus Island and the State Department's reply.
subfiles.from: Roland D. Hussey; E. Wilder Spaulding
subfiles.summary: Professor Roland D. Hussey of UCLA wrote to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on April 23, 1940, requesting information on whether the United States or Japan held title to Marcus Island in the Pacific. Internal routing notes prepared a response under the signature of Dr. E. Wilder Spaulding, Chief of the Division of Research and Publication. On May 4, 1940, Spaulding replied that Marcus Island is not claimed by the United States, is recognized as Japanese territory known as Minami-Torishima, and had been leased to a Japanese subject since the turn of the century.
subfiles.title: Inquiry and Reply Regarding the Status and Claims to Marcus Island
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs; Roland D. Hussey

subfiles.about: Chronological historical summary listing milestones of Japanese territorial expansion from 1879 to 1940.
subfiles.from: State Department
subfiles.summary: A multi-page chronological outline documenting Japan's progressive territorial acquisitions and policy statements from 1879 through 1940. It traces the annexation of the Bonin and Ryukyu Islands, Formosa, Sakhalin, Port Arthur, Korea, the German Pacific mandates, Kiaochow, and Manchuria, through to the 1937 invasion of China and the 1939 annexation of the Spratly Islands. The summary concludes with 1940 declarations regarding the New Order in Greater East Asia, Burma, and the South Seas region.
subfiles.title: Summary of the Japanese Territorial Expansion Program

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch and departmental memoranda regarding Japanese Foreign Office economic maps intercepted in Cuba.
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith; Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.summary: Ambassador George S. Messersmith transmitted three identic maps obtained from the Director of Cuban Posts that were being sent through the mails by the Japanese Foreign Office to its missions abroad. Internal memoranda show that the State Department analyzed the maps ('Outline of Present Day Economic and Commercial Conditions') and distributed copies to the Office of Naval Intelligence and the Military Intelligence Division. Stanley K. Hornbeck noted in a personal letter to Messersmith that the map placed occupied China and Thailand in the 'yen-bloc' and illustrated the economic resources of the South Seas.
subfiles.title: Transmittal and Intelligence Evaluation of Japanese Foreign Office Economic Maps Intercepted in Cuba
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; George S. Messersmith; ONI; MID

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Foreign Minister Toyoda taking issue with U.S. terminology regarding the Japanese occupation of Indochina.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: A cross-reference note referencing Telegram No. 1089 from Ambassador Grew in Tokyo (filed under 740.0011 European War 1939/314). It records that the new Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs insisted Japan harbored no territorial ambitions and objected to the United States' use of the term 'occupation' regarding Japanese military moves into French Indochina.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Japan Has No Territorial Ambitions / Indochina Move

subfiles.about: Consular despatch reporting the municipal incorporation of Tarumi-cho and Shioya-mura into the City of Kobe.
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner (American Consul, Kobe)
subfiles.summary: Consul Gerald Warner reports that the town of Tarumi, including Shioya village, was officially incorporated into the City of Kobe on July 1, 1941. The merger added 24,000 residents, raising Kobe's population above 1,000,000 and restoring its ranking as Japan's fifth-largest city ahead of Yokohama. Warner notes that because Shioya is now within Kobe city limits, consular officers stationed in Kobe no longer require special authorization to reside there.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 175: Inclusion of the Town of Tarumi in the City of Kobe

subfiles.about: Memorandum analyzing press reports regarding the extent of Japanese claims in the South China Sea known as Shinnan Gunto.
subfiles.from: Edwin O. Reischauer (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Drafted by Edwin O. Reischauer, this memorandum evaluates a New York Times article reporting that new Japanese maps showed unexpected territorial annexations in the South China Sea under the designation Shinnan Gunto. Reischauer points out that the geographic scope on the new maps does not exceed the boundaries formally notified to the State Department by the Japanese Embassy in March 1939, which extended within fifty miles of Palawan. The memo concludes that popular confusion stems from conflating the wider group of reefs with Spratly Island proper, and that no further U.S. diplomatic protest is required.
subfiles.title: The Extent of the Island Groups Claimed by Japan under the Name Shinnan Gunto
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Donation of a map of Japan marked with oil refineries and storage depots by an American citizen, forwarded to ONI.
subfiles.from: Paul C. McCready; George Atcheson, Jr.
subfiles.summary: Following the outbreak of war, Paul C. McCready of Bartlesville, Oklahoma, sent the State Department a detailed map of Japan marked with the locations of oil refineries and storage depots provided to him by a Japanese contact during past commercial negotiations. George Atcheson, Jr., Assistant Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledged the contribution with gratitude. The Department promptly forwarded a copy of the letter and map to the Office of Naval Intelligence for military use.
subfiles.title: Submission and Referral to Naval Intelligence of Map Indicating Japanese Oil Refineries and Depots
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Paul C. McCready; ONI

subfiles.about: FBI report on a intercepted delivery of Japanese cultural society maps to the Japanese Embassy, transferred to the War Department.
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover (Director, FBI)
subfiles.summary: FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover informed Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr., that FBI agents intercepted an American Express shipment from the Japanese Institute in New York to the Japanese Embassy on the evening of December 8, 1941. An examination with U.S. Army Engineers and Military Intelligence revealed sixty 1937 maps of Japan and adjacent regions published by Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai. At the request of the Army Engineers, who found the maps extremely valuable for operational planning, the State Department authorized their release to the War Department.
subfiles.title: Interception and Release to the War Department of Japanese Maps Consigned to the Japanese Embassy

subfiles.about: Legal and historical inquiry regarding whether the mandate over Pacific islands east of the Philippines arose from Versailles or Washington.
subfiles.from: Joseph T. Dillard; E. Wilder Spaulding
subfiles.summary: Joseph T. Dillard, an Oklahoma lawyer, inquired whether the former German Pacific islands east of the Philippines were mandated to Japan under the Treaty of Versailles or at the 1921-1922 Washington Disarmament Conference. After internal review by Division of Research and Publication staff, Dr. E. Wilder Spaulding provided a comprehensive factual reply explaining that the mandate was assigned by the Supreme Council of Allied and Associated Powers in May 1919 and confirmed by the League of Nations in December 1920. Spaulding enclosed the bilateral Yap Treaty of February 11, 1922, which resolved U.S. rights regarding the mandate outside the League framework.
subfiles.title: Inquiry and Detailed Departmental Reply Concerning the Origin of the Japanese Pacific Mandate

subfiles.about: Consular despatch forwarding a propaganda map distributed by the Japanese Embassy in Buenos Aires depicting conquests through 1942.
subfiles.from: Leonard Ware (First Secretary of Embassy, Buenos Aires)
subfiles.summary: First Secretary of Embassy Leonard Ware transmitted a copy of a map issued in late January 1943 by the Japanese Embassy in Buenos Aires displaying Japanese conquest claims through December 31, 1942. Ware noted that local Japanese press organs reacted with outrage because the map labeled place names in English rather than Japanese. He also observed that the original edition highlighted Japan, Chosen, and Taiwan in red, but doubted it achieved widespread distribution.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8528: Japanese Map of Their Conquests Through 1942

subfiles.about: Temporary loan and return of Naval Intelligence geographic monograph ONI-60 on Nanpo Shoto.
subfiles.from: A. V. S. Pickhardt (ONI); David McK. Key (State Dept)
subfiles.summary: Captain A. V. S. Pickhardt of the Office of Naval Intelligence forwarded a copy of classified geographic monograph ONI-60 (Part I - Nanpo Shoto) upon the oral request of Mr. Chamberlin of the State Department's Division of Political Studies. State Department liaison staff acknowledged receipt on April 19, 1943. On April 24, 1943, Assistant Liaison Officer David McK. Key formally returned the confidential monograph to ONI after its review.
subfiles.title: Loan and Return of Geographic Monograph ONI-60 (Nanpo Shoto)
subfiles.to: Orme Wilson; A. V. S. Pickhardt

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a congressional inquiry regarding territories seized by Japan since 1930.
subfiles.from: Patman-Wright
subfiles.summary: A cross-reference sheet indexing a letter dated May 7, 1943, from Patman-Wright (filed under 800.0146/71). The letter requested an authoritative statement from the Department of State disclosing all territories taken by Japan since 1930.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Request for Statement on Territories Taken by Japan Since 1930

subfiles.about: Transmittal of a captured Japanese world and commercial shipping map recovered from an evacuated Japanese resident in Manzanillo.
subfiles.from: Henry A. Hoyt (Vice Consul, Manzanillo)
subfiles.summary: American Vice Consul Henry A. Hoyt transmitted a fragment of a Japanese world map retrieved from the closed hardware store of Hachiro Naitoh in Manzanillo, Mexico. Hoyt reported that Naitoh, an influential local resident and reputed Major in the Japanese Army, had been ordered evacuated to the interior of Mexico in March 1942. Departmental geographers annotated the despatch noting that the document was an incomplete commercial shipping promotional map.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 98: Transmittal of Japanese Map Found in Manzanillo, Mexico

subfiles.about: Offer by Mrs. Roger B. C. Johnson to donate tourist literature and maps from a 1926 trip to Japan, and the Department's polite decline.
subfiles.from: Mrs. Roger B. C. Johnson; Joseph W. Ballantine
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Roger B. C. Johnson of Kittery Point, Maine, wrote offering to send travel folders and a large map of Japan acquired during a 1926 visit. Joseph W. Ballantine, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, replied on July 5, 1943, thanking her for her patriotic offer. However, he declined the materials because outdated tourist pamphlets published by the Japanese Government Railways were already available, though noting the Department remained interested in more recent, non-public materials.
subfiles.title: Correspondence with Mrs. Roger B. C. Johnson Regarding 1926 Japanese Travel Literature
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Mrs. Roger B. C. Johnson

subfiles.about: Despatch forwarding personal Japanese city maps from First Secretary Richard F. Boyce and State Department instructions returning them.
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce; Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: First Secretary Richard F. Boyce submitted several personal maps from his consular service in Japan, including detailed plans of Tokyo, Yokohama, Kyoto, Nagoya, and Shimoda Harbor, for military evaluation. On February 1, 1944, the Department sent an instruction back to Havana returning Boyce's personal maps as requested. The instruction noted that two copies of the map of Shimoda Harbor were permanently retained for government use.
subfiles.title: Submission and Return of Personal Japanese City and Harbor Maps of Richard F. Boyce
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; American Mission, Havana

subfiles.about: Navy Department request for State Department research studies on the Japanese Mandated Islands and transmittal thereof under strict secrecy.
subfiles.from: H. L. Pence; Orme Wilson; Harley A. Notter
subfiles.summary: Captain H. L. Pence of the Chief of Naval Operations (Office for Occupied Areas) requested copies of a 50-page State Department digest and legal appendix concerning the Class 'C' mandated Pacific islands for operational planning. Orme Wilson consulted Harley A. Notter, Chief of the Division of Political Studies, who authorized the release of a folder containing seven studies on January 5, 1944. Notter stipulated that the papers were strictly secret, did not represent final State Department policy, and could not be cited or attributed outside the Navy Department.
subfiles.title: Naval Request and Secret Transmittal of Studies on the Japanese Mandated Islands

subfiles.about: Transmittal by citizen J. T. Bullen of a Japanese promotional pamphlet and railway map regarding Manchuria.
subfiles.from: J. T. Bullen
subfiles.summary: J. T. Bullen of the East Baton Rouge Parish Department of Public Works sent Secretary of State Cordell Hull a Japanese English-language pamphlet distributed years earlier to American Rotary Clubs. Bullen noted that the pamphlet contained detailed Japanese railway maps of the region and offered it for military or geographic reference during the ongoing war effort.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of Japanese Pamphlet and Railway Map of Manchuria

subfiles.about: Internal State and War Department routing slips and memoranda coordinating the retention and examination of Boyce's Japanese maps.
subfiles.from: Sophia A. Saucerman; David McK. Key; Edward H. Miller
subfiles.summary: This group of routing slips and memoranda documents the inter-departmental handling of the maps submitted by Richard F. Boyce from Havana. Acting Geographer Sophia A. Saucerman advised that the maps could be sent to the War Department and retained one Japanese copy of Shimoda Harbor for the State Department collection. On December 30, 1943, David McK. Key forwarded the materials to Major Edward H. Miller of the Military Intelligence Division, while G-2 routing slips recorded transferring maps between the Army Map Service and departmental collections.
subfiles.title: Internal Departmental Memos on Processing and Evaluating Maps from Embassy Havana
subfiles.to: Liaison Officer; Major Edward H. Miller; Sophia A. Saucerman

subfiles.about: Transmittal of Admiral Leahy's letter advocating sole U.S. sovereignty over Japanese Mandated Islands and copies of 1917 secret Anglo-Japanese accords.
subfiles.from: John D. Hickerson; William D. Leahy; Sir Conyngham Greene
subfiles.summary: John D. Hickerson forwarded to Abbot Low Moffat a crucial letter of March 11, 1944, from Admiral William D. Leahy writing for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, alongside the secret February 1917 Anglo-Japanese exchange of notes regarding German island possessions. Leahy asserted that the Japanese Mandated Islands formed an indivisible strategic entity vital to American defense and must be placed under exclusive U.S. sovereignty without sharing control with allies like Australia or New Zealand. The 1917 diplomatic notes revealed Britain's wartime pledge to support Japanese claims north of the equator in exchange for Japanese support of British claims south of the equator.
subfiles.title: Joint Chiefs of Staff Recommendation for Sole U.S. Sovereignty over Japanese Mandated Islands
subfiles.to: Abbot Low Moffat; Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Policy memorandum proposing a clear statement on the wartime legal status and postwar disposition of the Japanese Mandated Islands.
subfiles.from: Abbot Low Moffat
subfiles.summary: Abbot Low Moffat urged Director Joseph C. Grew and the State Department Policy Committee to approve a definitive declaration concerning the status of the Japanese Mandated Islands. The memorandum was prompted by an application from a Hawaiian fertilizer firm to Interior Secretary Harold L. Ickes seeking exclusive phosphate mining licenses in the occupied islands. Moffat argued that the U.S. should explicitly reaffirm that military conquest does not convey legal sovereignty and that their international status will be settled only after the war, balancing legal principles with American security imperatives.
subfiles.title: Wartime Status and Post-War Disposition of Japanese Mandated Islands

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting intelligence on the withdrawal of Japanese troops from Portuguese Timor.
subfiles.from: State Department / Portugal
subfiles.summary: A cross-reference sheet indexing Telegram No. 2870 from Portugal dated September 14, 1944 (filed under 753.94/9-1444). The telegram conveys confidential information regarding the reported withdrawal of Japanese military forces from Timor.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Information with Regard to Withdrawal of Japanese from Timor

subfiles.about: Letter from Admiral Leahy to Norman H. Davis outlining post-war strategic island requirements in the Pacific.
subfiles.from: William D. Leahy (for Joint Chiefs of Staff)
subfiles.summary: Writing for the Joint Chiefs of Staff in September 1942 (formally transferred to State Department files in late 1944), Admiral William D. Leahy responded to Norman H. Davis regarding post-war security needs in the Pacific. Leahy emphasized that Japan must be stripped of all islands south of latitude 30 degrees North—specifically the Marshall, Caroline, Palau, Bonin, and Mariana groups, as well as Formosa—to secure Allied control over trans-Pacific air and sea routes. He also advised that the U.S. should avoid committing itself to any territorial dispositions until post-war strategic conditions were fully clarified.
subfiles.title: Joint Chiefs of Staff Statement on Post-War Security Needs and Island Disposition in the Pacific

subfiles.about: Despatch forwarding photographs of restricted areas in Japan donated by Chinese resident Kevin T. H. Wu, and transmittal to MID.
subfiles.from: Edward L. Reed (Chargé d'Affaires a.i., Buenos Aires)
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Edward L. Reed reported that Kevin T. H. Wu, a Chinese national residing in Argentina and former partner in a Buenos Aires curio shop, donated three photographs and negatives of sensitive locations in Japan where photography was prohibited. Reed noted Wu's desire to aid the Allied war effort, and the State Department forwarded the prints and negatives to the Military Intelligence Division on October 11, 1944.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 161: Photographs of Places in Japan Contributed by Chinese Resident of Argentina
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Military Intelligence Division

subfiles.about: Citizen offer of industrial and harbor maps of Osaka Bay and Kobe by former Stanley Works officer Ethelbert Allen Moore.
subfiles.from: Ethelbert Allen Moore; Otto E. Guthe
subfiles.summary: Ethelbert Allen Moore of New Britain, Connecticut, informed the State Department that he possessed several maps of the industrial area around Osaka Bay and Kobe acquired while planning a factory there for The Stanley Works. Otto E. Guthe, Acting Chief of the Division of Geography and Cartography, responded on December 8, 1944, welcoming the offer and enclosing a franked shipping label to send the maps for intelligence review.
subfiles.title: Correspondence with Ethelbert Allen Moore Concerning Industrial Maps of Osaka and Kobe
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Ethelbert Allen Moore

subfiles.about: Military Intelligence Service receipt confirming incorporation of Kevin T. H. Wu's photographs into the War Department terrain library.
subfiles.from: Edward H. Miller (Lt. Colonel, GSC, MID)
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Edward H. Miller, Liaison Officer for the Military Intelligence Service, informed State Department Liaison Officer A. Dana Hodgdon that the three photographs of Japan supplied by Kevin T. H. Wu were accessioned into the War Department library for terrain photography. Miller conveyed the Army's appreciation for the useful intelligence contribution.
subfiles.title: War Department Acknowledgment of Terrain Photographs Donated by Kevin T. H. Wu

subfiles.about: Offer of a folding travel map of Japan, Chosen, and Formosa by Harry White, and the Department's polite decline.
subfiles.from: Harry White; Erle R. Dickover
subfiles.summary: Harry White of Buffalo, New York, wrote to describe a detailed folding tourist map of the Japanese Empire and cities that he purchased in 1934 during a trip from Nagasaki to Tokyo, offering it to the government. Erle R. Dickover, Chief of the Division of Japanese Affairs, replied on November 11, 1944, thanking him for his patriotic generosity but stating that the Department already possessed ample copies of that standard tourist edition.
subfiles.title: Correspondence with Harry White Regarding 1934 Tourist Map of the Japanese Empire

subfiles.about: Transmittal and official distribution of four Japanese maps of Kobe and Osaka presented by The Stanley Works.
subfiles.from: R. E. Pritchard; S. W. Boggs
subfiles.summary: President R. E. Pritchard of The Stanley Works formally transmitted four Japanese maps of Kobe, Osaka, and neighboring industrial areas pursuant to earlier correspondence. On February 22, 1945, Chief Geographer S. W. Boggs acknowledged receipt and reported their disposition: three maps were incorporated into the State Department's working cartographic collection, while a detailed 1:20,000 scale map of Kobe by the Japan Tourist Bureau was transferred to the Library of Congress.
subfiles.title: Donation and Distribution of Japanese Maps of Kobe and Osaka by The Stanley Works
subfiles.to: Otto E. Guthe; R. E. Pritchard

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting transmittal of a proposed financial directive and accounting guide for the Japanese Outlying Islands.
subfiles.from: Navy Department
subfiles.summary: A cross-reference sheet indexing a communication of December 19, 1944, from the Navy Department (filed under 894.5151/12-1944). The document forwards a proposed financial directive and basic accounting guide for the administration of the Japanese Outlying Islands.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: Proposed Financial Directive and Accounting Guide for Japanese Outlying Islands

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet acknowledging State Department concurrence in the Proposed Economic Directive for the Japanese Outlying Islands.
subfiles.from: Navy Department
subfiles.summary: A cross-reference sheet referencing a letter dated December 20, 1944, from the Navy Department (filed under 894.5151/12-2044). The letter acknowledges receipt of the State Department's December 16 concurrence regarding the Proposed Economic Directive for the Japanese Outlying Islands.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: State Department Concurrence in Economic Directive for Japanese Outlying Islands
